drills.q: What is a Bar Raiser, and what power do they hold?
drills.a: A trained interviewer from a different team than the hiring one, whose job is keeping the bar consistent by probing past your rehearsed layer, and who holds VETO power over the decision.

drills.q: How many LP questions should you expect in an Amazon loop, and how are they distributed?
drills.a: Roughly 12-15. Four to five back-to-back interviews, each interviewer assigned two to three specific LPs so the panel collectively covers all sixteen. Every round also has a technical component. Prepare two stories per heavily weighted LP, not one great story overall.

drills.q: Name the four LPs that cluster heaviest in engineering loops, and your lead story for each.
drills.a: Dive Deep (the OOM on 1.2M rows), Deliver Results (4.5h to 30min, ~89%), Invent and Simplify (3,447 Java lines removed for an 812-line Python service), Bias for Action (automating market risk pipelines from a Business Analyst seat).

drills.q: What does Amazon's Principal Engineering tenets material say about Deliver Results, and what replaces it as the bar?
drills.a: Deliver Results is a LOW BAR for a Principal Engineer. The bar is lasting impact that echoes through technology, product and company; clarity from complexity with problems framed in customer and business context; hands-on leading by example; educating the organisation about trends and approaches.

drills.q: Which two Amazon LPs have no story in this resume, and what is the fix?
drills.a: Hire and Develop the Best, and Strive to be Earth's Best Employer. Fix: write one real, small story each. Onboarding someone onto the platform, raising the code review bar, the 200+ tests as an enabling artifact for others, a runbook that stopped a recurring page, or running interviews. Small and true beats large and invented.

drills.q: Why does vagueness fail at Google specifically?
drills.a: Because the decision is made by a hiring committee who never interviewed you and reads only the written evidence packet. Anything that does not survive transcription (rapport, energy, the interviewer's general sense of competence) evaporates. Speak in complete sentences with the odd specific numbers: 54,486, 3,447, 307, 178,000.

drills.q: Name Google's four attributes and say what GCA is actually scoring.
drills.a: Role-Related Knowledge, General Cognitive Ability, Leadership, Googleyness. GCA scores whether your reasoning is structured and adaptive, not whether the answer was right, which is why announcing your reasoning structure aloud is itself evidence.

drills.q: Give a Googleyness story that would actually score, and one that would not.
drills.a: Scores: going back to your own service-decomposition criterion and testing each boundary against it rather than defending the design, with deploy coupling as the evidence. Does not score: saying you value intellectual humility, or a trivial regret with no cost. Googleyness must come through described behaviour, not stated values.

drills.q: Describe the Meta E6 onsite and the pre-onsite round.
drills.a: Onsite: one standard coding, one AI-assisted coding, one architecture, one design, one behavioural. Before the onsite, a Leadership Assessment interview replaces the standard phone screen at E6 and is roughly half behavioural and half coding. E7+ adds deeper design, deeper behavioural, and a cross-functional round graded on judgment under ambiguity.

drills.q: 'How do you work with AI coding tools, and when did you override one?' Give the shape of a passing answer.
drills.a: Where you use them (boilerplate, test scaffolding, unfamiliar API surfaces); where you do not (anything with a concurrency or authorization invariant); how you verify (tests you wrote yourself, reading the diff not the summary, a category rule about what you will not accept unread); then one concrete override with the reason. The authorization and concurrency work are exactly the categories where generated code is most dangerous.

drills.q: What is the Meta E6 scope bar, and which of your stories clear it?
drills.a: A disagreement must involve two or more TEAMS on a large project; impact must be on the ORG, not the team. Candidates that clear it: the credential mechanism across a service fleet, Query Crafter serving non-technical stakeholders in other functions, the Credit Suisse automation from a non-engineering seat, and Skillmaster integrated into another team's provisioning platform. Do not inflate the single-team stories; use a different one.

drills.q: What is Microsoft's As Appropriate round, how do you read it, and what should you do between rounds?
drills.a: The final round, usually a Principal Engineering Manager or Partner-level leader, tailored to your earlier performance with interviewers syncing notes first. Relaxed and pitching the team = sell mode. Aggressively probing gaps = borderline. Between rounds, write down your weakest answer and prepare the second pass; almost nobody does this and it is nearly free.

drills.q: Which four stories lead at Microsoft, and why is it the best fit on the list?
drills.a: 22-locale hardening (global readiness), cross-tenant authorization (multi-tenant security), Java-to-Python migration (legacy modernisation with a safe cutover), skill resolution engine (domain depth). Best fit because Microsoft's actual world is enterprise multi-tenancy, compliance, backward compatibility and migration of installed customers, which is where most of this resume sits.

drills.q: What must you rehearse for Netflix that no other loop demands?
drills.a: Verbal architecture with no whiteboard: number the components, state direction explicitly since there are no arrows, name them once and reuse the names. Multiple candidates report completing the Netflix system design round with no diagramming tool at all.

drills.q: How does the Netflix framing change your story delivery relative to Amazon?
drills.a: Candour is scored positively, so leading with 'eight services was too many, here's what I'd do instead' lands well. Do not over-structure: rigid STAR reads as corporate. Expect fewer prompts and keep talking through silence. Be willing to disagree with the interviewer once, well. At Amazon the same candour needs a completion: what you'd do instead and the trigger for the change.

drills.q: Describe the OpenAI loop and say where your prep effort should go.
drills.a: Resume screen, recruiter call, role-specific skills assessment, gate-format technical screen (one problem escalating across ~4 stages, usually need to clear at least two), a PAID 48-hour work trial graded on shipping speed, code quality, design choices and tests, then a loop of four to six. Prep goes to the work trial: practise implement-to-spec then refactor as constraints are added, with tests. Polishing behavioural answers for this loop is misallocated.

drills.q: 'Why did you self-host instead of using an API?' Answer for an AI lab, including the gap.
drills.a: Volume growth against linear per-token pricing, plus tenant data-handling expectations. Critically: not self-host everything, but split by workload shape (self-hosted vLLM online, Bedrock batch offline, hosted frontier for tasks that need it). The gap, stated directly: no dollar break-even model was built; you optimised for throughput and control. Then offer the derivation live rather than inventing a percentage, because an interviewer who runs GPU capacity knows the numbers.

drills.q: 'What's your view on multi-agent systems?' Take a defensible position and survive the follow-up.
drills.a: Position: most multi-agent systems are one agent with extra latency and an ambiguous failure mode; the test is whether failure modes, scaling profiles or deploy cadences genuinely differ. Then your own system as evidence, including the accepted cost (network boundaries, distributed failure model, tracing to debug one run). Follow-up 'are you defending your own?': name the merge candidate (transcript processing and chunking, same input, always sequential) and what stays separate (gap detection, different trigger and cadence).

drills.q: Which metric set do you use in which room?
drills.a: Product set (2M+ users, ~25% engagement, 50% report turnaround) for Amazon, Meta and Microsoft. Systems set (throughput, cost per million tokens, p99, 1.2M rows, ~2.5 GB index, KV-cache-bound concurrency) for AI labs and infrastructure roles. Know which set applies within the first thirty seconds of a round.

drills.q: When should you NOT apply company-specific tailoring?
drills.a: Do not name a Leadership Principle while telling the story: exhibit the behaviour, do not narrate the rubric. Do not memorise mission statements; know the loop and the rubric instead. Do not apply structured STAR at a twelve-person startup. Do not lead with product metrics for an infrastructure role. And never let tailoring override truth: if Meta wants multi-team scope and your story is single-team, use a different story rather than inflating, because inflated scope collapses on 'which teams, and what did they want?'
